v.why: Replacing a parameter-free pooling op on the final edge into the output node with a 3x3 conv adds useful capacity, more so than replacing none or skip (e.g. exp 9).
When node 1 is already conv-processed, a conv on edge 1->3 is largely redundant; gains are big only when edge 0 is none/skip/pool (exps 32-34 vs 31, 35-39).
Swapping a 3x3 conv for avg pooling removes learnable capacity on the edge between the intermediate nodes (exps 41, 49).
Replacing skip with pooling costs little or even helps, whereas replacing a conv costs a lot (exps 42, 50 vs 41).
Upgrading a pooling edge into node 2 to a conv adds capacity, whereas replacing skip/none often disrupts gradient flow (exp 54 vs 51, 53).
Deleting a conv on the edge from node 2 to the output loses capacity, whereas deleting pool or skip is neutral or helpful (exps 71, 79 vs 74, 75).
Removing a conv on the first edge removes a learnable path, more harmful than removing skip/pool/1x1 (domain prior; exps 22 vs 25-28).
Replacing a conv on edge 1->3 with an identity loses capacity, while replacing none/1x1/pool is neutral or positive (exps 91, 95, 98 vs 92-94, 96).
Replacing pooling into the output with a skip yields a clean residual path and large gains (exp 93).
Removing a harmful pooling edge into the output helps far more than removing a conv (exp 75 vs 71, 79).

Reading of the 100 experiments:

- **Avoid the extreme values.** Very large swings (±20 to ±75 pp) come from connectivity changes: the cell is cut off or reconnected from input to output. These are degenerate, not real interactions, so I put little weight on them.
- **Replacing a strong op.** Swapping a 3×3 convolution for pooling, skip or none usually hurts the edit's effect.
- **Replacing a weak op.** Swapping avg_pool for something else usually helps.
- **Redundant paths.** When another path already does the same job, edits on edge 4 matter less.
